AI_C01_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
Karma, taken together with the knowledge that has the lower (apara) Brahman as its object, has been concluded. That supreme path of karma combined with knowledge has been wound up by way of the meditation on the Uktha. This (Prāṇa, the lower Brahman) is the truth, the Brahman called Prāṇa. This is the one Deity. All the gods are but the manifold splendours of this very Prāṇa. It has been said that one who attains the nature of this Prāṇa thereby attains the divinities themselves. This very absorption-into-the-deities (devatā-apyaya) is held by some to be the supreme human goal — this is liberation, and this alone is to be reached by the means already laid down, namely the conjoint practice of knowledge and karma; beyond this, they say, there is nothing higher. Wishing to refute these, the subsequent section, beginning with "Ātmā vā idam," is begun for the sake of enjoining the knowledge of the Self alone, unconnected with karma.

Objection: How is it ascertained that the subsequent text is for the purpose of enjoining the knowledge of the Self alone, divorced from karma?

Reply: Because no other purpose can be made out from it. Moreover, the text is going to demonstrate that the previously mentioned deities — Agni and the rest — are themselves transmigratory, since they too are afflicted by hunger and thirst, as in "He afflicted it with hunger and thirst" (Ai. Up. 1.2.1). Whatever is subject to hunger and the rest is nothing but saṃsāra; for of the supreme Brahman the Śruti declares the absence of hunger and so on.

Objection: Granted that the knowledge of the Self alone is the means to liberation; still here it is only the agent of karma (karmin) that is qualified for it, since no specific qualification (for renunciation) is mentioned, and since no other āśrama outside the karmin's path is mentioned in this text. Indeed, having begun with the karma characterised by the Bṛhatī-sahasra, immediately thereafter the knowledge of the Self is taken up. Therefore the karmin alone is the qualified one. Nor is the knowledge of the Self unrelated to karma, because it is wound up at the end as before. Just as in the case of the karmin (the worshipper) the identity of the Puruṣa, who has the sun for his Self, with all beings — moving and unmoving — was stated in both the Brāhmaṇa and the Mantra portions by "Sūrya is the Self" (Ṛk Saṃ. 1.115.1) and the rest, in just the same way, beginning with "This is Brahman, this is Indra" (Bṛ. Up. 3.1.3) and so on, the Self-hood of all beings is taught, and is concluded with "Whatever is unmoving, all this has prajñā for its eye" (Bṛ. Up. 3.1.3). Likewise the Saṃhita Upaniṣad, in "For the Bahvṛcas meditate upon this very one in the Mahā-uktha" (Ai. Ār. 3.2.3.12) and so on, after stating its connection with karma, concludes with "In all beings they speak of this very one as Brahman." Furthermore, of the very same one — described as "the bodiless prajñā-Self" — oneness has been declared in "And one should know that the sun yonder is one and the same as this." Here too, beginning with "Who is this Self?" (Ai. Up. 3.1.1), the Śruti will show its very nature as the prajñā-Self by "Prajñāna is Brahman" (Ai. Up. 3.1.3). Therefore the knowledge of the Self is not unrelated to karma.

Objection: Then surely there is the defect of repetition — for the Self that has already been ascertained by the Brāhmaṇa passage "Verily, I am Prāṇa, O Sage" and by the Mantra "Sūrya is the Self," is again, with the question "Who is this Self?" (Ai. Up. 3.1.1), being ascertained afresh through the Brāhmaṇa beginning "Ātmā vā idam." This is repetition and so purposeless.

Reply: Not so; it serves to ascertain certain other particular attributes of that very same Self, hence there is no fault of repetition. How? Because it serves to ascertain particular attributes of that very Self — connected with karma — namely, His being the cause of the creation, sustenance and dissolution of the world; or else it is for the sake of pure upāsanā alone; or again, this latter section beginning with "Ātmā" is meant to convey that, since for the karmin the upāsanā of the Self apart from karma has not been obtained — not having been enjoined in the context of karma — therefore the Self by Itself is also fit for upāsanā. And since the Self is to be meditated upon both as differentiated and as non-different, even though in the context of karma the view of difference
AI_C01_S01_V01: Verily, in the beginning all this was the Self, one alone; nothing else whatsoever was active. He bethought Himself: "Let Me create the worlds."
AI_C01_S01_V01::block-0:
"Ātmā" — Ātman is so called from the roots āp (to pervade), at (to eat / consume), or atati (to go continuously); He is supreme, omniscient, omnipotent, free from hunger and all the other attributes of saṃsāra, eternal, ever-pure, ever-awakened, ever-free in His very nature, unborn, undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless, and non-dual. "Idam" — this entire universe, differentiated by name, form and karma. He, the Self alone, was the One in the beginning, that is, prior to the creation of the world.

Objection: Is He not even now that very One alone?

Reply: He is. Then why is it said "He was"? Although even now He alone is the One, still there is a distinction. Prior to creation, the world existed with name and form undifferentiated, identical with the Self, fit only for the cognition and word "Self," "One"; whereas now, having its name-and-form differentiated, the world is the object of many words and cognitions as well as still being the object of the single word and cognition "Self" — this is the distinction. Just as foam, before its name and form become distinguished from water, is the object only of the single word and cognition "water," but when, separating from water, it becomes differentiated by its own name and form, then the same water and foam are the objects of many words and cognitions, while remaining also (as foam viewed in essence) the object of the single word and cognition "water" — exactly so here.

"Nānyat kiñcana miṣat" — nothing else whatsoever, having the activity even of a winking eye, nor anything inert. Not, as the Sāṃkhyas hold, an independent Pradhāna inclined to the side of the non-Self; not, as the Kāṇādas (Vaiśeṣikas) hold, atoms — no such thing other than the Self existed here. What then? The intent is: only the Self, one alone, was. "Saḥ" — He, by His very nature of being all-knowing, the Self, being one alone, ekṣata — saw, considered.

Objection: How could He see prior to creation, when there was no body and no sense organs?

Reply: This is no fault, on account of His being all-knowing by very nature. So too the Mantra: "Without hands and feet He grasps and is swift" (Śve. Up. 3.19) and so on. With what intention did He see? The text says: "Lokān nu sṛjai" — "Let Me create the worlds — Ambhas and the others — which serve as places for the experiencing of the fruits of beings' karma."
AI_C01_S01_V02: He created these worlds: Ambhas, Marīcis, Mara, and the Āpas. The Ambhas is yonder, beyond the heaven; heaven is its support. The Marīcis are the inter-space. Mara is the earth. The waters are those beneath.
AI_C01_S01_V02::block-0:
Having thus seen, that is, having reflected, He, the Self, created these worlds — He produced them. Just as a skilful craftsman, a carpenter or the like, having reflected, "Let me build palaces of such-and-such kind," forthwith builds palaces, exactly so.

Objection: It is reasonable for a carpenter and the like, who has material at hand, to construct palaces; but how can the Self, who has no material, create the worlds?

Reply: This is no fault. Name and form, undifferentiated, identical with the Self — comparable to the foam-stage in water — and fit to be designated by the single word "Self," can well serve as the material cause for the world, which is comparable to the differentiated foam. Hence, being Himself the upādāna of name-and-form which are not other than His own Self, the omniscient One fashions the world — there is no contradiction. Or rather, just as a magician (māyāvin), endowed with knowledge but with no external material, fashions himself, as it were, into another self moving through the sky, so the omniscient God, all-powerful, the great wielder of māyā, fashions His very Self into another self in the form of the universe — this is the more apposite view. And on this view none of the doctrines that the effect alone is real, or the cause alone, or both, or neither, find any room — they are all clearly refuted.

Which worlds did He create? "Ambho marīcīr maram āpaḥ." In the order of ākāśa and the rest, having brought into being the Cosmic Egg, He created Ambhas and the rest of the worlds. Among them, the Śruti itself explains "Ambhas" and the rest. "Adaḥ" — that, which is denoted by the word ambhas, the world, "pareṇa divam" — beyond the heavenly world, that is what is meant by ambhas, because it sustains (bharaṇa) the waters (ambhas). "Dyauḥ pratiṣṭhā" — the heaven is the support, the foundation of that ambhas-world. The mid-region (antarikṣa), which is below the heavenly world, is the marīcis. Though one, it is grammatically plural because of the multiplicity of stations, hence "marīcayaḥ"; or it is so called from its connection with the rays (marīci, raśmi). "Pṛthivī maraḥ" — earth, in which beings die (mriyante) — hence mara. "Yā adhastāt" — those that are below the earth, those are called "āpaḥ," being lokas, derived from āp (to pervade). Although the worlds consist of all five elements, still, because water (ap) predominates, they are spoken of by water-names alone — "ambho marīcīr maram āpaḥ."
AI_C01_S01_V03: He bethought Himself: "Here now are the worlds; let Me create the world-protectors." From the very waters He drew forth a Puruṣa and gave him form.
AI_C01_S01_V03::block-0: Having created the four worlds, which serve as the substrata for the experiencing of the fruits of the karmas of all beings, the Lord again reflected: "These worlds — Ambhas and the rest — that I have created, would, if left without protectors, perish; therefore, for their protection, let Me create lokapālas, protectors of the worlds." Having so seen, He, "adbhya eva" — from the very waters, that is, from those very five elements, of which water is the principal one, from which He had created Ambhas and the rest, from those very same — "puruṣaṃ" — a person, having the shape of a man, possessed of head, hands and so on, "samuddhṛtya" — having taken up out of the waters, just as a potter takes up a lump of clay from the earth — "amūrchayat" — He gave him solid form, He compacted him, that is, by joining together his limbs.
AI_C01_S01_V04: He brooded on him. From him, brooded upon, the mouth burst open as an egg; from the mouth, speech; from speech, fire. The nostrils burst open; from the nostrils, prāṇa; from prāṇa, vāyu. The eyes burst open; from the eyes, sight; from sight, the sun. The ears burst open; from the ears, hearing; from hearing, the quarters. The skin burst open; from the skin, the hairs; from the hairs, the herbs and the trees. The heart burst open; from the heart, the mind; from the mind, the moon. The navel burst open; from the navel, apāna; from apāna, death. The generative organ burst open; from it, the seed; from the seed, the waters.
AI_C01_S01_V04::block-0: "Tam" — Him, that pinda, of human shape, fixing upon, He brooded — that is, He performed abhidhyāna, He resolved upon him; for the Śruti says "whose tapas is of the nature of knowledge" (Mu. Up. 1.1.9). Of that pinda, brooded upon by the tapas of the Lord's saṅkalpa, the mouth burst open — there arose a hollow of the shape of the mouth, just as in the case of a bird's egg the egg bursts open. From the mouth, thus split open, vāk — the organ of speech, an indriya — issued forth; its presiding deity is Agni; thence, from speech, the lokapāla. So too the two nostrils burst open. From the nostrils, prāṇa; from prāṇa, vāyu. Thus everywhere the triad — adhiṣṭhāna (location), karaṇa (organ), and devatā (deity) — emerges in succession. So too the eyes, the ears, the skin, the heart (the seat of the inner organ), the mind (the inner organ itself), and the navel — the place of the binding-together of all prāṇas. Because of its conjunction with apāna it is called "apāna," the organ of evacuation; hence its presiding deity is Mṛtyu (death). Just as before, so the generative organ burst open — the seat of the procreative indriya. The indriya, the seed, on account of its purpose of emitting seed, is mentioned together with the seed itself. From the seed, the waters.
AI_C01_S02_V01: These deities, thus created, fell into this great ocean. He afflicted him (the Puruṣa) with hunger and thirst. They (the deities) said to Him: "Find us an abode wherein, established, we may eat food."
AI_C01_S02_V01::block-0:
These very deities, Agni and the rest, sanctioned by the Lord as lokapālas and so created, fell into this great ocean — the ocean of saṃsāra: vast, with avidyā, kāma and karma giving rise to its waters of sorrow; with fierce diseases, old age and death as its mighty crocodiles; beginningless, endless, shoreless, supportless; whose only resting-place consists in the petty pleasures born of the contact of the senses with their objects; in which rise up hundreds of mighty waves of misfortune stirred up by the gusts of the winds of thirst for the five sense-objects; in which the great roar that rises from the howling and lamenting of those who have fallen into the manifold hells, beginning with the great Raurava — "alas! alas!" — sounds aloud; whose sole boat is filled with knowledge for its provisions, the provisions being the qualities of the Self such as truth, uprightness, charity, compassion, non-injury, calm, restraint, fortitude and the rest; whose path is association with the holy and the renouncing of all; and whose far shore is mokṣa — into this very great ocean did they fall, that is to say, were plunged. Therefore the path described as the absorption of the deities Agni and the rest, fruit of the conjoint practice of knowledge and karma, is itself unable to bring about the cessation of the sufferings of saṃsāra — this is the intent here.

Since this is so, knowing this thus, one ought to know, for the cessation of all the sorrows of saṃsāra, that supreme Brahman, the Self of one's own self and of all beings, possessed of the qualifications about to be described, established as the cause of the origination, sustenance and dissolution of the world. For "This is the path, this is karma, this is Brahman, this is satya" (Ai. Up. 2.1.1) — namely this very knowledge of the supreme-Brahman-as-Self — and as the Mantra declares: "There is no other path for liberation" (Śve. Up. 3.8; 6.15).

"Tam" — Him, the Puruṣa, the pinda, the seed-source of the body, the senses and the deities, first produced by Him as the embodied Self, He associated with hunger and thirst — "anvavārjat" means He united (Him with them), He made them follow Him. Because that very causal Puruṣa is afflicted with the defects of hunger and the rest, the deities also, which are His effects, are subject to hunger and so on. Thus afflicted by hunger and thirst they said to Him, the Grandsire, the Creator: "Find out for us — that is, ordain for us — an āyatana, an abode, wherein, established, equipped, we may eat food."
AI_C01_S02_V02: He brought a cow to them. They said: "Verily this is not enough for us." He brought a horse to them. They said: "Verily this is not enough for us."
AI_C01_S02_V02::block-0: Thus addressed, the Lord, taking up another lump from the very same waters as before, kneading it and giving it form, brought to those deities a "gām" — a lump of the shape of a cow — and showed it. They again, having seen the form of the cow, said: "Verily this — for us, that is, for our sake of taking up an abode for the eating of food — this pinda is not 'alam,' not adequate, not fit for our being established in." "Alam" means sufficient; the meaning is: it is not fit for eating-from. The cow being thus rejected, He likewise brought to them a horse. They again said, "Verily this is not enough for us," exactly as before.
AI_C01_S02_V03: He brought a man (Puruṣa) to them. They said: "Ah, well done!" — for verily the Puruṣa is well-made. He said to them: "Enter, each into your proper abode."
AI_C01_S02_V03::block-0: When all (other forms) had been rejected, He brought to them a Puruṣa, fashioned of their very own womb-substance. They, on seeing the Puruṣa, their own native source, free from sorrow, said: "Su kṛtaṃ bata" — "Ah! well-made indeed is this abode!" Therefore the Puruṣa alone — "puruṣo vāva sukṛtam" — is the well-made one, since he is the cause of all meritorious karma; or else, sukṛta, because he is fashioned by the Lord Himself, by His own Self, by His māyās. To those deities the Lord, knowing this abode to be desirable to them, said — for indeed all rejoice in their own native abodes — "yathāyatanaṃ" — to that abode, of each, which is fit for the activities such as speaking and so on — "praviśata" — enter ye.
AI_C01_S02_V04: Fire became speech and entered the mouth; air became prāṇa and entered the nostrils; the sun became sight and entered the eyes; the quarters became hearing and entered the ears; the herbs and trees became hair and entered the skin; the moon became mind and entered the heart; death became apāna and entered the navel; the waters became semen and entered the generative organ.
AI_C01_S02_V04::block-0: Having received the consent ‘So be it,’ as in a city the chief of the army and others receive the king’s sanction, Agni — the deity that presides over speech — became speech itself and entered his own seat, the mouth. The remaining cases are to be construed in the same manner. Vāyu entered the nostrils, the sun entered the eyes, the quarters entered the ears, the herbs and trees entered the skin, the moon entered the heart, death entered the navel, and the waters entered the generative organ.
AI_C01_S02_V05: To Him hunger and thirst said: ‘Find an abode for us also.’ He said to them: ‘I assign you a share in these very deities; I make you sharers along with them.’ Therefore, to whichever deity an oblation is offered, hunger and thirst become sharers in that very deity.
AI_C01_S02_V05::block-0: When the deities had thus obtained their seats, hunger and thirst, being themselves without any abode, addressed Him — the Lord — saying: ‘Devise, contemplate, ordain a seat for the two of us as well.’ The Lord, thus addressed, said to those two, hunger and thirst: ‘It is not possible that you, being non-sentient in your own form, should obtain the function of consuming food without resorting to some sentient substratum. Therefore, I bestow upon you a share, that is, I favour you with an apportionment of function, in these very deities — Agni and the rest, both as adhyātma (within the body) and as adhidaivata (among the cosmic powers). Whatever share, in the form of oblation and the like, belongs to whichever deity, by that very share I make the two of you, hunger and thirst, sharers along with them.’ Since the Lord ordained thus at the beginning of creation, even now, to whichever deity an oblation in the form of caru, puroḍāśa and the like is taken up for the sake of that deity, hunger and thirst become sharers, that is, possessors of a share, in that very deity.
AI_C01_S03_V01: He thought: ‘Here are the worlds and the guardians of the worlds; let me create food for them.’
AI_C01_S03_V01::block-0: He, the Lord, thus reflected. How? ‘These worlds and the guardians of the worlds have been created by Me, and they have been linked with hunger and thirst. Hence their continuance is not possible without food. Therefore let Me bring forth food for these guardians of the worlds — sṛjai means sṛje, let Me create.’ For in worldly experience too, freedom in granting favour and in inflicting restraint is seen on the part of lords with regard to their own dependants. Likewise, in the case of the great Lord also, since He is the Lord of all, there is freedom alone with respect to all in matters of favour and restraint.
AI_C01_S03_V02: He brooded over the waters, and from those that were brooded over, a form was born. That form which was born — that, verily, is food.
AI_C01_S03_V02::block-0: He, the Lord, desiring to create food, brooded with reference to those very waters previously mentioned. From those waters, brooded over and standing as the material cause, was born a form — solid, capable of being grasped, characterised as the moving and the unmoving. That form which was thus born is, verily, food.
AI_C01_S03_V03: That, when thus created, sought to flee away. He sought to grasp it with speech, but he could not grasp it with speech. If he had grasped it with speech, then by merely uttering food one would have been satisfied.
AI_C01_S03_V04: He sought to grasp it with prāṇa (the breath), but he could not grasp it with prāṇa. If he had grasped it with prāṇa, then by merely smelling food one would have been satisfied.
AI_C01_S03_V05: He sought to grasp it with the eye, but he could not grasp it with the eye. If he had grasped it with the eye, then by merely seeing food one would have been satisfied.
AI_C01_S03_V06: He sought to grasp it with the ear, but he could not grasp it with the ear. If he had grasped it with the ear, then by merely hearing food one would have been satisfied.
AI_C01_S03_V07: He sought to seize it [the food] with the skin; he could not grasp it with the skin. Had he indeed seized it with the skin, then merely by touching food one would have been satisfied.
AI_C01_S03_V08: He sought to seize it with the mind; he could not grasp it with the mind. Had he indeed seized it with the mind, then merely by thinking of food one would have been satisfied.
AI_C01_S03_V09: He sought to seize it with the generative organ; he could not grasp it with the generative organ. Had he indeed seized it with the generative organ, then merely by emitting one would have been satisfied with food.
AI_C01_S03_V10: He sought to seize it with the apāna (down-breath); he caught it. This indeed is the seizer of food, namely the vāyu (air). Verily, the air is that which lives upon food — yes, this air.
AI_C01_S03_V10::block-0:
That food, having been created facing the worlds and the world-guardians as that which they should partake of, just as a mouse and the like, finding itself within the field of view of cats and the like, thinks 'Death — the eater of me — is here,' and turns away — being averse, going aslant (parāk), it sought to overleap and escape the eaters; that is, it began to flee. Perceiving this intent of the food, that lump (piṇḍa) — having the character of the aggregate of the worlds and world-guardians together with their effects and instruments — being himself the first-born and seeing no other eaters of food, sought to seize that food by speech, by the activity of utterance. He could not — he was not able — to grasp, to take hold of, that food by speech, by the act of speaking. Had that first-born embodied one indeed seized that food by speech, then the entire world, being the effect of speech, would have been satisfied with food merely by uttering it. But this is not so. Hence we understand that even the first-born was unable to grasp it by speech.

The sequel is parallel: he sought to seize the food by that breath, by that eye, by that ear, by that skin, by that mind, by that generative organ — by the activity of each respective instrument — and being unable to grasp the food, afterwards, by the down-breath (apāna), by the wind, through the orifice of the mouth, he sought to seize the food, and seized it (tadāvayat) — that is, he ate it. Therefore that down-breath (apāna-vāyu) is the 'seizer of food,' the apprehender of food. The vāyu — the air which is well known as 'living upon food' (annāyu), having food as its bond, having food as its sustenance — that very air is this.
AI_C01_S03_V11: He reflected: 'How could this [body-aggregate] subsist without me?' He reflected: 'By which of the two [paths] shall I enter?' He reflected: 'If speech utters, if the breath breathes, if the eye sees, if the ear hears, if the skin touches, if the mind meditates, if the apāna draws down, if the generative organ emits — then who am I?'
AI_C01_S03_V11::block-0:
He, having thus established the standing of the world-and-world-guardian aggregate by means of food — like the master of a city contemplating the standing of the city, its citizens and its protectors — reflected: 'How — in what manner — could this, without me, the master of the city, exist? This effect of the body-and-organ aggregate, about to be described, how indeed could it, being for-another's-sake (parārtham), exist without me?' If [it functions on its own], that is, if there were merely the activities of speech and the rest — 'if [there is] uttering by speech' and so on — then it would by no means be purposeless: it would be like the homage and the like rendered by the citizens and prisoners, which is for the master's sake but useless if there be no master, that is, if the master be unreal. By the same reasoning, then, there must be a Master — myself — superior, presiding (adhiṣṭhātṛ), the witness (sākṣin) of what is done and not done as fruit, the experiencer (bhoktṛ) — just as a king is for the city. Even granting that this aggregate is for-another's-sake, it would still presuppose me, the seeker for whom it exists, the conscious one, the protector — without whom it cannot stand, just as the affairs of the city and its citizens cannot stand without their master.

'Then who am I, of what nature, master of what?' If, having entered the body-and-organ aggregate, I should not apprehend the fruits of the activities of speech and the rest — as a king, having entered a city, takes cognizance of the deeds and omissions of the appointed officers — then no one would discover or examine that 'I am, and am of such-and-such a nature.' But in the contrary case, that very one who knows 'this is uttered by speech' and so on — he is to be discovered as 'I am' and as having the form of pure knowing (vedana-rūpa), for whose sake this 'uttering' and the rest of the conjoined organs of speech etc. exist. Just as the pillars, walls, and the rest, conjoined as a palace, exist for the sake of another not conjoined with their own constituent parts, so likewise [these organs exist for me]. Having thus reflected, [he asks] 'By which of the two shall I enter?' The 'fore-foot' (prapada) and the 'crown of the head' (mūrdhan) are the two paths of entry into this aggregate; 'by which of these two paths shall I enter (prapadyai) this city, characterized as the body-and-organ aggregate?'
AI_C01_S03_V12: Cleaving this very partition (sīman), he entered through this door. This indeed is the door called Vidṛti — that is the place of bliss (nāndana). For him there are three abodes, three dreams: 'this is an abode, this is an abode, this is an abode.'
AI_C01_S03_V12::block-0:
Having thus reflected: 'I shall not enter through the soles, by the entry-path of my servant, the prāṇa, who is appointed to all my purposes; rather, by way of elimination (pāriśeṣya), splitting open the crown of his head, I shall enter — even as men in the world enter [their houses by the upper door]' — that very Lord (īśvara), the creator who acts after due reflection (īkṣitakārī), cleaved this very partition of the crown — the boundary where the parting of the hair ends — making an opening, and through this door, by this path, entered (prāpadyata, praviveśa) this body-and-organ aggregate. This indeed is the well-known door, since when oil and the like are poured upon the crown the inner taste of that liquid is felt within. This very [door], from being thus split open, is named Vidṛti — well known as such. The other doors — the ear and the rest — being common pathways assigned to the [organs of] retainer-status, are not abundant (samṛddhi), not sources of bliss. This door alone is the Supreme Lord's own. Hence it is nāndanam — verily, the place of nandana (bliss). The lengthening 'nāndanam' is Vedic licence (chāndasa). 'By this door, going on, one rejoices (nandati) in the supreme Brahman.'

For that one who, having thus created and entered, like a king his city, by means of this jīva (which is in truth the Self), there are three abodes (āvasathāḥ): in the waking state, the right eye as the seat of the senses; in dream, the inner mind; in deep sleep, the space within the heart — these are the three. Or [as will be stated below], the three abodes are: the body of the father, the womb of the mother, and one's own body. And the three dreams (svapnāḥ) are those known as waking, dream, and deep sleep.

Objection: But the waking state, being of the form of full awareness, is not a 'dream.' — Not so; it too is precisely a dream. How? Because of the absence of awakening to the supremely-real own-Self, and because, like a dream, what is seen is unreal (asad-vastu-darśanāt). 'This is the abode' — namely the right eye — is the first; the inner mind is the second; the space within the heart is the third. The repetition 'this is the abode' merely restates what was stated. For in these abodes, [the jīva], existing alternately as if it were the Self (ātmabhāvena), is, by natural avidyā, deeply asleep for a long time, and does not awaken even when struck by the hammer-blows of sufferings born of the impact of many hundreds of thousands of evils.
AI_C01_S03_V13: Being born, he distinguished the beings [thinking]: 'What other [than the Self] could one here even speak of?' He saw this very Person, the Brahman, the most pervaded, [exclaiming]: 'I have seen This!'
AI_C01_S03_V13::block-0: He, being born — having entered the body as the jīvātman — distinguished (vyākarot) the beings. At some time, when the supremely compassionate teacher (paramakāruṇika ācārya) struck the great kettle-drum of Vedānta — that producer of the awakening sound of Self-knowledge — close to his ear, he awoke to, and saw, this very Puruṣa lying within the city (puri-śayāna), the Self, who has been the topic [of the foregoing] as the agent of creation and the rest, [knowing him as] Brahman — vast (bṛhat) — most-pervaded (tatatama, where, with one elision of the letter 'ta,' the word stands for 'tata-tama' = vyāptatama, fully complete, like ākāśa). How? '[Saying] this Brahman, the very own-form (svarūpa) of my Self, I have seen — Aho!' The lengthening (pluti) at the end is for the sense of [exclamatory] reflection.
AI_C01_S03_V14: Therefore his name is Idandra ('It-seer'). Idandra indeed is his name. Him, who is Idandra, [the wise] call 'Indra' indirectly (parokṣeṇa); for the gods are, as it were, fond of indirect names — yes, the gods are, as it were, fond of indirect names. Thus the third section.
AI_C01_S03_V14::block-0: Because [he saw it] saying 'idam' (this), as something direct, not indirect — i.e., he saw the Brahman, the innermost of all (sarvāntara), as immediate (sākṣāt, aparokṣa), and not mediately — therefore, since 'he sees this' (idaṁ paśyati), the supreme Self is named 'Idandra.' 'Idandra' indeed is the well-known name of the Lord (īśvara) in the world. Him, who is thus Idandra, [the knowers of Brahman] designate as 'Indra' indirectly (parokṣeṇa) — by an indirect appellation — for purposes of common usage (saṁvyavahārārtham), out of fear of taking the direct name, since [the Lord] is most worthy of worship. For the gods are, as it were (iva), fond of indirect [names] — fond of the use of indirect names — for [such is their nature]. How much more, then, would the God of all gods, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), [be such]! The repetition (dvirvacana) is for the conclusion of the present chapter.
AI_C02_S01_INTRO1::block-0:
In this chapter the import of the text is as follows. The Self — author of the world's origin, sustenance and dissolution, untouched by saṃsāra, omniscient, all-powerful, all-knowing — created this entire world by Himself in the order beginning with ākāśa, without taking recourse to any other substance distinct from Himself. Then, for the sake of awakening His own Self, He Himself entered all the bodies endowed with prāṇa and the rest. And having entered, He directly cognised His own Self exactly as it is — "This Brahman am I." Therefore He alone is the one Self in all bodies, and there is no other. Elsewhere too it has been declared, "He is my Self; thus let one know — I am Brahman," and "Verily, this was Ātman alone in the beginning" (Ai. U. 1.1.1), and "Brahman is the most pervasive" (Ai. U. 1.3.13). And in another place: of the Self who is all-pervading, the Ātman of all, there is not even a hairsbreadth left unentered — how then could He, splitting open a fissure, enter, like an ant entering a burrow?

Now it may be objected: this objection is far from trifling; much more is to be objected here. "Without organs, He saw" — yet seeing presupposes organs. "Without taking up anything, He created the worlds" — yet creation presupposes material. "Drawing the Puruṣa up from the waters He shaped him" — and "by His meditation the mouth and other parts were cleft open, and from mouth and the rest arose Agni and the other lokapālas." Their conjunction with hunger and the rest, their seeking an abode, the showing of the cow and other forms for that purpose, their entering each into its proper station, the flight of the food once created, and the desire of speech and the other deities to seize it — all this stands on a footing exactly like the splitting of a fissure to enter.
AI_C02_S01_INTRO1::block-1:
"Then let all this be incoherent." Not so. Since here only the awakening to the Self is intended to be conveyed, all this is arthavāda (subsidiary praise-statement); hence there is no fault. Or it may be likened to a magician: the supreme Lord, the great wielder of māyā, omniscient and omnipotent, fashioned all this for the easy comprehension and apprehension (of the Self), as is done in worldly narratives and the like — this is the more reasonable position. For no fruit is sought from the mere knowledge of the creation-narrative and the rest; whereas from the knowledge of the form of the unity of the Self, the fruit, namely immortality, is universally established in all the Upaniṣads. And in the Smṛtis, in the Gītā and elsewhere: "the supreme Lord standing equal in all beings" (Bh. Gī. 13.27), and so forth.

[Pūrvapakṣa:] But there are three Selves. The jīva, the enjoyer, the doer, the saṃsārin, is one — well established in all worldly and scriptural usage. By the mark, namely the construction of the world's body which is fit to serve as the manifold seat of the fruits of the deeds of many beings, just as palaces and the like are constructed (their builder being inferred) — the world's maker is inferred to be a second conscious Self, an Īśvara who is omniscient and skilled in the relevant craft, like a carpenter. Third is the Puruṣa of the Upaniṣads, established by texts like "that whence words turn back" (Tai. U. 2.4.1) and "not thus, not thus" (Bṛ. U. 3.9.26). These three Selves are mutually distinct. How then can it be known that there is but one Self, non-dual, free from saṃsāra?

[On the jīva itself:] How indeed is even the jīva known? — "He is known thus: hearer, thinker, seer, instructor, smeller, cognizer, knower." But this is self-contradictory: the very one who is doer of hearing and the rest is said to be "unthought-of, yet the thinker; uncognized, yet the cognizer." So too: "Thou canst not think the thinker of thinking; thou canst not cognize the cognizer of cognition" (Bṛ. U. 3.4.2). True, it would be self-contradictory if He were known by direct perception, like pleasure and the like; but perceptual knowledge is precisely what is forbidden by "not the thinker of thinking," etc. He is known, however, through the inferential mark of hearing and the rest — where then is the contradiction?

[Refutation of even this:] But how is He known even through such marks? For when the Self hears the sound to be heard, then, being engaged in the act of hearing alone, the acts of thinking and cognizing are not possible — neither in that Self, nor in another. Likewise with the acts of thinking and the rest. And the acts of hearing and so on operate only upon their own objects: thinking by the thinker is not possible apart from a thinkable. — "But for the mind, everything whatever is thinkable." True; yet even all that is thinkable cannot be thought without a thinker. — Suppose so; what follows? — This: He who is the thinker of all is just the thinker, and would not Himself be thinkable; nor is there a second thinker for the thinker. If He is to be thought by the Self alone, then the Self by which He is thought and the Self who is thought become two; or one Self splits in two as thinker and thought, like a piece of bamboo cleft asunder. Either way, it is impossible — just as two lamps cannot stand to each other as illuminator and illumined, being equal. Nor is there any moment when the thinker is free of the thinking-operation upon a thinkable, so as to use it for self-thinking. And even when the thinker thinks the Self through some mark, then too, as before, the Self that is thought through the mark and the thinker thereof become two — or one becomes two — and the same fault follows. Hence neither by perception nor by inference is He known.
AI_C02_S01_INTRO1::block-2:
How then is there knowledge of Him as "He is my Self"? Tell me by what method I am to know Him as "He is my Self." Here they tell a tale. A certain bewildered man, when on some occasion of fault he was told by some, "Fie on you! you are no man," — out of his bewilderment, in order to convince himself of his own manhood, approached someone and said, "Sir, tell me who I am." The other, knowing his bewildered state, said, "I shall enlighten you step by step." Setting aside the notion of his being stationary objects (stones, plants) and the rest, he said only, "You are not a non-man," and stopped. The bewildered fellow replied, "You set out to enlighten me and now you have fallen silent — why do you not enlighten me?" Such precisely is your objection. He who, even on being told "He is not a non-man," does not grasp his own manhood — how, even on being told "You are a man," would he grasp his own manhood? Therefore the method of awakening to the Self is exactly the scriptural instruction, and no other. For grass and other combustibles fit for fire's burning cannot be burnt by anything else.

This is precisely why scripture, having set out to make known the Self's own nature, having said as it were by the negation of non-manhood, "Not thus, not thus" (Bṛ. U. 3.9.26), then ceased. So too the teaching, "without inside or outside" (Bṛ. U. 2.5.19; 3.8.8), "this Ātman is Brahman, the all-experiencing" (Bṛ. U. 2.5.19); "That thou art" (Chā. U. 6.8.7), "but where for him all has become the very Self, then by what should one see what?" (Bṛ. U. 2.4.14; 4.5.15), and the like.

As long as one does not know this Self as taught, so long, taking the upādhi characterised by the non-Brahman view as the Self and, through avidyā, regarding the upādhi's properties as belonging to the non-Self, one revolves again and again through stations from Brahmā down to a clump of grass, transmigrating under the sway of avidyā, kāma and karman. So transmigrating, he abandons the body-and-organ aggregate he has assumed; abandoning, he takes up another; and again and again, like the unbroken current of a river, with the unbroken sequence of birth and death — through what stages does he pass? Showing this very theme as a ground for vairāgya, the śruti speaks —
AI_C02_S01_V01: Verily, this (jīva) first becomes an embryo in a man. That which is this seed is the vigour gathered together from all the limbs; verily, in his own self he bears the self. When he sheds it into a woman, then he generates it. That is his first birth.
AI_C02_S01_V01::block-0: This very transmigrant — afflicted with avidyā, kāma, karman and self-conceit — having performed sacrifices and the like, departing from this world by the path of smoke and the rest, reaches the moon, and when his karman is exhausted, by the path of rain and so on reaches this world; becoming food, he is offered into the man-fire (puruṣāgni). "Verily, in that man" — this saṃsārin first, primarily, becomes an embryo in the form of seed by the sequence of essence (rasa) and the rest. This the text states: "that which is this seed in the man, by that very form." And this seed is the essence-form, the very pith, gathered together (sambhūta) and ripened from all the limbs — that is, from all the constituents of the food-formed body characterised as rasa and so on. Being the very Self of the man, that seed is termed Ātman; that Self, taking the form of an embryo as seed, he bears, that is, supports, in his own self, that is, in his very own body. "When he sheds that seed into a woman" — when his wife is in her season, into the woman-fire that is the woman, he sheds it, approaching her; "then he generates it" — then the father generates this seed which is his own self in the form of an embryo. That issuing forth from his station, in the form of seed at the time of seminal emission, is for this saṃsārin his first birth, the first manifestation of his states. This very thing has already been said earlier in passages such as "That Self [generates] this self," etc.
AI_C02_S01_V02: It (the seed) attains identity with the woman, just like one of her own limbs; therefore it does not injure her. She nourishes this self of his that has come into her.
AI_C02_S01_V02::block-0: That seed, when shed into the woman, attains to her ātmabhūya — non-difference from her own self — just as it had been with the father; that is, it reaches her in the manner of "like one of her own limbs," such as the breast and the rest — exactly so. For this reason that embryo does not injure this mother as a tumour and the like would do. Since it has come to share her self-hood like a limb of her own, namely the breast and so on — for that very reason it does not injure, does not hurt her: such is the meaning. She, being pregnant, having understood that this self of her husband has come into her, that is, has entered her womb, "nourishes" — makes him grow, protects him — by avoiding food and the rest that are injurious to the embryo and by employing food and so forth that are favourable.
AI_C02_S01_V03: She, the nourisher, becomes one to be nourished. The woman bears that embryo. He (the father) cherishes the boy from the very moment of birth onwards. In that he cherishes the boy from the very moment of birth, he therein nourishes only his own self for the continuance of these worlds — for thus indeed are these worlds continued. This is his second birth.
AI_C02_S01_V03::block-0:
She, being the nourisher (bhāvayitrī), the one who makes the husband's self, who has become an embryo, grow, becomes herself one to be nourished by the husband — for in the world no relation between any two stands without mutual benefit and reciprocation. The woman bears that embryo by the prescribed regimen of carrying the foetus, before its birth. He, the father, even before — at the very moment of birth — cherishes the new-born boy by the jātakarman and other rites: "from the moment of birth onwards." In that the father, by the jātakarman and other ceremonies, nourishes the boy thus born, just-born, immediately at birth — in so doing he is nourishing only his own self; for the father's very Self is what is born in the form of the son. This too has been declared: "the husband enters his wife" (Hari. 3.73.71) and the like.

But to what end does he beget his self in the form of a son and nourish him? It is said: "for the continuance of these worlds" — that is, for their non-interruption. For these worlds would be cut off were men not to perform the begetting of sons and so forth. Since these worlds endure as a continuum precisely by the unbroken sequence of begetting children and other duties, therefore for their non-interruption that is to be done — but not for the sake of mokṣa: such is the meaning. Here Śaṅkara silently marks the pravṛtti-mārga (continuance of worlds through procreation) as distinct from the nivṛtti-mārga of liberation. That issuing forth of this saṃsārin from the mother's womb in the form of a boy is, with reference to the previous seed-form, his second birth — the manifestation of the second state.
AI_C02_S01_V04: He (the son), this self of his (the father's), is set in his place for the meritorious works (he is to perform). And this other self of his (the father), having fulfilled his duties, advanced in age, departs. Departing from here, he is born again. That is his third birth.
AI_C02_S01_V04::block-0:
Of this father, this same son-self is "set in place" for the prescribed meritorious works — that is, in order to accomplish them, he is appointed in the father's stead, as one who is to perform what the father is to do. So too, in the Sampratti-vidyā of the Vājasaneyaka: "Instructed by his father, [the son says] 'I am Brahman, I am the sacrifice,' and so on — he takes them up" (Bṛ. U. 1.5.17).

Then, having lodged his own burden upon the son, the other self of this son's father — that is, the father's self — having become "kṛtakṛtya," namely freed from the threefold debt and having accomplished what was to be done, advanced in age, aged, "departs," namely dies. He, departing from here, that is, abandoning this body, taking up another body laden with karman just as a worm or leech does, is born again. That third existence which he has yet to attain after dying — that is the third birth.

[Objection:] But the saṃsārin's first birth was reckoned from the transmigrating father by way of seed; that same one's second birth was said to be in the form of a boy, from the mother. When the third birth is to be spoken of, why is the father's own departure-and-rebirth called the third birth?

[Reply:] No fault. For it is intended that father and son share one self. That son too, in his turn, lodging his burden upon his own son, departing from here, is born again, like his father. So, what has been said in one place is, by śruti's intention, said in the other also — owing to the identity of self of father and son.
AI_C02_S01_V05: This has been declared by the seer: "While yet in the womb, I came to know all the births of these gods. A hundred iron strongholds guarded me; yet, like a hawk, with swift force I broke forth." Vāmadeva, while still lying in the womb, spoke thus.
AI_C02_S01_V05::block-0: Thus transmigrating, mounted upon the unbroken sequence of birth and death through the manifestation of the three states, the entire world is fallen into the ocean of saṃsāra. Whenever, by some means, in any state whatsoever, one comes to know the Self as taught in śruti — at that very moment one becomes one whose every saṃsāric bond is loosed and who is kṛtakṛtya: this fact has been declared by a seer in a mantra also. Hence the text says: "While yet in the womb of the mother, even when within the womb-receptacle" — "nu" being a particle of reflection — "by the maturing of meditation through many former births, of these gods — speech, fire and the rest — I came to know all (viśva) the births (janimāni)" — that is, "oh, I have awakened to them." "A hundred — that is, many — iron strongholds (āyasīḥ puraḥ) — bodies as it were impenetrable like iron — guarded me, holding me from issuing out of the bonds of saṃsāra." "Then, like a hawk piercing the net, with swift force (javasā) generated by the power of self-knowledge, I have flown forth." — Behold! Vāmadeva, the seer, while still lying in the womb, declared this.
AI_C02_S01_V06: He, knowing thus, having ascended upward from the breaking-up of this body, having attained all desires in that heavenly world (the supreme Self), became immortal — became immortal. Thus ends the Fourth Section.
AI_C02_S01_V06::block-0: He, the seer Vāmadeva, knowing thus the Self as declared, from this "breaking of the body" — that is, from the breaking-up brought about by the upamarda of the seed of bodily origination, namely avidyā and the rest, by the power born of partaking of the nectar of the knowledge of the supreme Self; the breaking of the body, which is fashioned by avidyā, impenetrable as iron, beset by the unbroken series of bodies invaded by hundreds of misfortunes such as birth and death — that is, from the body's destruction. Becoming "upward," namely become the supreme Self, ascending from the downward existence which is saṃsāra, attaining the pure all-self-hood illumined by knowledge, in that "heavenly world" already described — undecaying, undying, immortal, fearless, omniscient, with no prior, with no posterior, without inside or outside, of one taste with the nectar that is prajñā — that is, in his very own Self, in his own form — he became immortal. By the knowledge of the Self, having already attained all desires (āptakāmatā) — even while living, having attained all desires — such is the meaning. The repetition (samabhavat samabhavat) is to indicate the conclusion of the knowledge of the Self with its fruit and its illustration.
AI_C03_S01_INTRO1::block-0: The brāhmaṇas of the present day, mumukṣus, jijñāsus of Brahman, having come to know the attainment of the fruit, namely the all-self-hood (sarvātma-bhāva), brought about by the means which is brahmavidyā — a fruit illumined by the unbroken traditional śruti coming through the lineage of teachers headed by Vāmadeva and others, and exceedingly well established in the assembly of the knowers of Brahman — and desiring to remove themselves from the saṃsāra characterised by the relation of means and end, which is non-eternal and reaches as far as the very condition of jīva-hood, deliberating with one another, ask one another. How? —
AI_C03_S01_V01: "Who is this Self upon whom we meditate? Which one is the Self — that by which one sees, or that by which one hears, or that by which one smells odours, or that by which one articulates speech, or that by which one discerns the sweet and the unsweet?"
AI_C03_S01_V01::block-0:
"Which Self is it that we meditate upon as 'This is the Self' directly? Who is that Self?" — that very Self which Vāmadeva, having directly meditated as 'This is the Self,' became immortal — "Him too let us meditate upon. Who indeed is that Self?" Thus, when they were questioning one another with the desire to know, there arose in them a recollection born of the latent impression of the previously taught Śruti concerning a particular subject — namely: 'Brahman entered this person through the soles of the feet,' and 'Having cleft this very crown, He entered through this door.' Two Brahmans entered this very person, taking on a relation of mutual contrariety. And these two are constitutive of the body. Of these two, one alone deserves to be the Self that is to be meditated upon. "Which is here the one to be meditated upon? Which one is that Self?" Thus, in order to determine the specific one, they questioned one another again, deliberating.

Further, as they deliberated, their understanding came to rest upon the very ground of specific inquiry. How? Two things are perceived in this body: the instrument differentiated into many divisions by which one apprehends, and the one who apprehends — the latter known by the connection of memory whose object was apprehended through other instruments. Of these, that by which one apprehends cannot be the Self. "By what, then, does one apprehend?" To this it is said: "That by which, becoming the eye, one sees form; that by which, becoming the ear, one hears sound; that by which, becoming the organ of smell, one smells odours; that by which, becoming the organ of speech, one articulates speech consisting of names such as 'cow' and 'horse,' and likewise 'good' and 'bad'; that by which, becoming the tongue, one discerns the sweet and the unsweet."
AI_C03_S01_V02: "That which is the heart and the mind — this. Cognition (saṃjñāna), command (ājñāna), discernment (vijñāna), full knowing (prajñāna), retentive intellect (medhā), perception (dṛṣṭi), steadfastness (dhṛti), thinking (mati), independent reflection (manīṣā), agitation (jūti), memory (smṛti), resolve (saṅkalpa), determination (kratu), vital activity (asu), desire (kāma), longing (vaśa) — all these indeed are names of prajñāna."
AI_C03_S01_V02::block-0:
"What, then, is that one instrument differentiated in many ways?" To this it is said. What was previously stated — 'The seed of beings is the heart, the seed of the heart is the mind, by the mind were created Waters and Varuṇa; from the heart, mind, and from the mind, the moon' — that very thing is this heart and mind. It is one alone, manifold-fold. By this single inner organ, becoming the eye, one sees form; becoming the ear, one hears; becoming the organ of smell, one smells; becoming speech, one speaks; becoming the tongue, one tastes; by its own form as imagining, it resolves as mind; by its form as heart, it determines. Therefore this single instrument is what operates in the spheres of all the instruments — for the apprehender, for the sake of all apprehension. So too among the Kauṣītakins: 'Having mounted speech by means of prajñā, by speech one obtains all names; having mounted the eye by means of prajñā, by the eye one obtains all forms' (Kauṣ. Up. 3.6) and so on. And in the Vājasaneyaka: 'For one sees by the mind alone, hears by the mind; by the heart alone one cognises forms' (Bṛ. Up. 1.5.3) and so on. Therefore the fact that what is denoted as 'heart-mind' is the instrument of all apprehension is well established.

And of that very nature is prāṇa, for the Brāhmaṇa says: 'That which indeed is prāṇa, that is prajñā; that which indeed is prajñā, that is prāṇa' (Kauṣ. Up. 3.3). And we have already stated, in the Prāṇa-saṃvāda and elsewhere, that prāṇa is of the nature of the aggregate of instruments. Therefore, that Brahman which entered through the feet — since it is, as the apprehender's instrument of apprehension, of secondary status (guṇa-bhūta) — that very entity, Brahman, cannot be the Self that is meditated upon. By the method of remainder, the apprehender — for whose apprehension the modifications of this heart-mind instrument, soon to be enumerated, exist — that apprehender is the Self that is to be meditated upon by us. This they decided.

Now are stated those modifications of the inner organ, having for their objects the inner and outer realities, which serve the apprehension of the apprehender — that is, of Brahman, of the form of prajñāna, situated under the limiting adjunct of the inner organ: saṃjñāna is full cognition, the state of being conscious; ājñāna is the state of commanding, lordliness; vijñāna is the specialised knowledge of the arts and the like; prajñāna is full knowing, the condition of insight; medhā is the capacity to retain texts; dṛṣṭi is the apprehension of all objects through the senses; dhṛti is that holding-up by which the body and senses, even when sinking down, are sustained — for they say, 'They bear the body by dhṛti'; mati is reflection; manīṣā is independence in such reflection; jūti is the mind's state of being afflicted by pain and the like; smṛti is recollection; saṅkalpa is the framing of forms as bright, dark, and so on; kratu is determination; asu is the activity that is the cause of the life-functions such as breathing; kāma is the thirst, the longing for an object not at hand; vaśa is the longing for sexual union and the like.

These and other such modifications of the inner organ — being for the sake of the apprehension of the apprehender — are limiting adjuncts of Brahman, whose nature is pure prajñāna; and the names saṃjñāna and the rest are designations of qualities born of these adjuncts. Therefore all of them are names of prajñāna, which is mere insight, and not directly its own. So too it has been said: 'When breathing, it is named prāṇa' (Bṛ. Up. 1.4.7) and so on.
AI_C03_S01_V03: "This is Brahman, this is Indra, this is Prajāpati; these are all the gods, and these five great elements — earth, air, ether, waters, lights; and these together with what is, as it were, mingled with the small. The seeds, both these and those — those born of eggs, those born of wombs, those born of sweat, and those born of sprouts; horses, cows, men, elephants, and whatever else is here that breathes — that which moves, that which flies, and that which stands still. All this has prajñā for its eye; it is established in prajñā. The world has prajñā for its eye; prajñā is its foundation. Prajñāna is Brahman."
AI_C03_S01_V03::block-0:
That very Self of the form of prajñāna is the lower Brahman, established in every body — Prāṇa, Prajñātmā — entered into the limiting adjuncts of the inner organs, like the reflection of the sun entered into divisions of water; that is Hiraṇyagarbha, Prāṇa, Prajñātmā. This very one is Indra — by virtue of qualities, or because he is king of the gods. This is Prajāpati who is the firstborn embodied one, from whom, by means of the cleaving of mouth and the rest, were born Agni and the other lokapālas — that Prajāpati is this very one. And those, Agni and the rest, all the gods, are this very one. And these five great elements — earth, etc. — which are the material causes of all bodies, characterised as food and food-eater, these too. Further, these others, of the form 'mingled, as it were, with the small' — small meaning slight — these are serpents and the like; the word 'iva' here is without independent meaning. Seeds — that is, causes — both these and those, indicated under a twofold division. Which are these? It is said: aṇḍaja, those born of eggs, namely birds and the like; jāruja, the womb-born — humans and so forth; svedaja, those born of sweat, lice and the like; udbhijja, those born by sprouting forth — trees and the like.

Horses, cows, humans, elephants, and whatever else here that breathes. What is that? Jaṅgama — that which moves, walking with feet; patatri — that which is given to falling through the sky; sthāvara — that which is unmoving. All this, without remainder, has prajñā for its eye. Prajñā is full insight; that itself is Brahman alone. That by which one is led is netra (eye); that whose eye is prajñā is prajñā-netra. It is established in prajñā, in Brahman, at the times of arising, abiding, and dissolution — that is, prajñā is its support. The world has prajñā for its eye, as before — or, the entire world has prajñā as its eye. Prajñā is the support (pratiṣṭhā) of the whole universe. Therefore, prajñāna is Brahman.

That very Brahman, when all distinctions of limiting adjuncts have set, is taintless, stainless, actionless, peaceful, one, non-dual, to be known by the negation of all distinctions through 'neti neti' (Bṛ. Up. 3.9.26), beyond the range of all words and notions. The same, by connection with the limiting adjunct of pure prajñā, is Īśvara, omniscient, the impeller of the unmanifest seed of the universe common to all, and from his ruling-ness is named the Inner Controller (Antaryāmin). That very one, marked by the conceit of being the cognitive self that is the seed of the manifest universe, is named Hiraṇyagarbha. That very one, with the limiting adjunct of the first body that arose within the cosmic egg, is named Virāṭ-Prajāpati. That very one, with the limiting adjuncts of Agni and the rest that arose from him, is named the deities. So too in the limiting adjuncts of particular bodies — from Brahmā down to a tuft of grass — Brahman attains those very respective names and forms.

That one alone, differentiated by all the divisions of the limiting adjuncts, is known and conceived in every manner manifoldly by all beings and by logicians. The Smṛti says: 'Some call him Agni, others Manu, Prajāpati; some Indra, others Prāṇa, others the eternal Brahman' (Manu 12.123) and so on.
AI_C03_S01_V04: "He, by means of this prajña-Self, ascending from this world, having obtained all desires in that heavenly world yonder, became immortal — became immortal." Thus the fifth section.
AI_C03_S01_V04::block-0: That Vāmadeva, or any other who knows Brahman as taught above by means of the prajña-Self — by that very prajña-Self by which the former knowers became immortal, even so this knower, by that very prajña-Self, ascending from this world, and so on, has been explained. Ascending from this world, in that heavenly world yonder, having obtained all desires, he became immortal, became immortal — Om.
